content.user_title: Price Data Products with Defensible Models
content.value_statement: Data products often lack clear costs, comparable offers, and stable buyer value. This skill builds evidence-based price ranges, commercial structures, and negotiation plans.
actual_capabilities: Calculates a pricing floor from data acquisition, processing, maintenance, opportunity costs, and a stated profit assumption.
Estimates buyer value through replacement cost, revenue gain, cost savings, or avoided loss.
Combines cost, value, and market evidence into a documented price range.
Compares buyout, usage, subscription, hybrid, revenue-share, and tiered pricing structures.
Designs anchor, target, and floor positions with decreasing concessions and non-price tradeoffs.
Drafts pricing strategies, comparison tables, quotation content, negotiation plans, and review recommendations.
limitations: It cannot verify confidential buyer inputs, internal costs, or unsupported market comparables.
It does not provide live market prices unless the user supplies current evidence.
Its price ranges depend on assumptions and require validation through customer research and negotiation.
It does not replace licensed valuation, legal, tax, regulatory, or competition advice.

use_cases.title: Launch a Data API
use_cases.description: Compare cost, buyer value, and market evidence before choosing a launch range and billing model.

use_cases.title: Prepare an Enterprise Quote
use_cases.description: Create anchor, target, and floor positions with concession rules for a complex buyer discussion.

use_cases.title: Review an Existing Price
use_cases.description: Assess cost, usage, customer value, and competitive changes before recommending a price adjustment.

prompt_templates.title: Estimate a Basic Price Range
prompt_templates.prompt: I sell [data product] to [buyer]. Costs are [costs], and expected buyer value is [value]. Estimate a price range and state assumptions.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this when initial cost and buyer value estimates are available.

prompt_templates.title: Choose a Pricing Structure
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare subscription, usage, tiered, and hybrid pricing for [product]. Recommend one model using [usage pattern], [update frequency], and [buyer constraints].
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this when the price level is known but the billing model is unclear.

prompt_templates.title: Build a Negotiation Plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Build anchor, target, and floor prices for [product] using [cost], [buyer value], and [market comparables]. Add decreasing concessions and non-price tradeoffs.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this before an enterprise pricing discussion.

prompt_templates.title: Create an Advanced Pricing Memo
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a pricing decision memo for [product] across [segments]. Apply cost, value, and market methods. Show sensitivities, compliance risks, evidence gaps, and review triggers.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this for cross-functional approval of a segmented pricing strategy.

output_examples.input: Annual costs are CNY 240,000. Target markup is 25%. Buyer savings are CNY 4 million. Comparable offers range from CNY 280,000 to 360,000.
output: Illustrative cost floor: CNY 300,000, assuming a 25% markup on annual costs.
Value reference: CNY 400,000 at a 10% share of buyer savings.
Recommended range: CNY 320,000 to 360,000, with a CNY 400,000 anchor and CNY 300,000 floor.

output_examples.input: The API receives seasonal traffic, updates weekly, and serves a buyer seeking low initial commitment.
output: Recommended structure: a base subscription plus tiered usage charges.
The base fee supports recurring update costs, while usage tiers align price with realized demand.
Set volume thresholds from observed usage and review them after the first contract period.

output_examples.input: An enterprise buyer says the quote is too expensive but will not share a budget.
output: Confirm whether the concern is affordability, uncertain value, scope, or competitive comparison.
Offer a limited pilot or narrower data scope before reducing the unit price.
Trade any concession for volume, term length, prepayment, reduced support, or narrower usage rights.

best_practices: Label every assumption, source, unit, time period, and confidence range used in the calculation.
Validate buyer value with customer evidence before selecting a value-share percentage.
Review prices every six to twelve months and after material changes in cost, quality, demand, or regulation.
anti_patterns: Do not use marginal delivery cost alone to price a reusable data product.
Do not present a precise price when buyer value or comparable evidence is weak.
Do not offer unplanned discounts without receiving a defined commercial concession.

faq.question: What information should I provide?
faq.answer: Provide cost components, buyer use cases, expected value, comparable prices, usage volume, update frequency, and commercial constraints.

faq.question: Does the skill guarantee a successful price?
faq.answer: No. It produces a defensible range, but actual willingness to pay must be tested with buyers.

faq.question: Which pricing structures can it compare?
faq.answer: It compares buyout, usage, subscription, base-plus-usage, license-plus-revenue-share, and tiered structures.

faq.question: Can it prepare a formal quotation?
faq.answer: It can draft pricing logic and quotation content. Legal, tax, payment, delivery, and usage terms still require professional review.

faq.question: Does it collect current market prices?
faq.answer: No. It analyzes market evidence supplied by the user and identifies gaps that require further research.

faq.question: When should a price be reviewed?
faq.answer: Review it every six to twelve months, or sooner after major changes in cost, quality, buyer value, demand, or regulation.
